articles.title: Denver Broncos cheerleader’s secret day job has fans completely amazed
articles.summary: NFL cheerleaders are known for balancing demanding schedules, but few stories have captured fans’ attention quite like that of Denver Broncos cheerleader Ann-Marie Muscarello.
articles.body:
NFL cheerleaders are known for balancing demanding schedules, but few stories have captured fans’ attention quite like that of Denver Broncos cheerleader Ann-Marie Muscarello.

Over the past several days, Muscarello has gone viral on social media after football fans discovered that her life extends far beyond the sidelines of Broncos games.

While many know her as one of the faces of Denver’s cheerleading squad on Sundays, her primary profession during the week is one that carries a very different kind of responsibility: she is a nurse.

The revelation has sparked admiration across social media, with fans praising Muscarello for successfully navigating two careers that demand energy, discipline, and an unwavering commitment to helping others.

articles.title: Broncos cheerleader’s double life reignites heated debate over low NFL pay
articles.standfirst: The Broncos cheerleader’s demanding schedule is highlighting a long-running debate over NFL cheerleader compensation
articles.summary: The Broncos cheerleader’s demanding schedule is highlighting a long-running debate over NFL cheerleader compensation
articles.body:
Denver Broncos cheerleader Ann-Marie Muscarello is giving NFL fans a glimpse into the demanding reality behind the glamour of professional football.

The veteran cheerleader recently shared a social media post showing the striking contrast between her Sundays on the sidelines and her Mondays working as an orthopedic nurse.

“Sunday mornings vs. Monday mornings look a little different,” Muscarello wrote on Instagram, alongside images highlighting her two very different careers. The post quickly attracted attention, with fans praising her work ethic while also questioning why NFL cheerleaders often need another job to make ends meet.

Many commenters described Muscarello as inspiring and impressive, particularly because she manages the physical demands of professional cheerleading while working in healthcare during the week.

Others focused on the financial side of the situation, arguing that women who dedicate their time to NFL franchises deserve substantially better compensation.

Muscarello’s circumstances aren’t unusual. Professional cheerleaders across the NFL have frequently balanced practices, games, appearances and promotional commitments with full-time careers, education or other responsibilities. Cheerleading is a passion and a dream for many rather than a job capable of providing a primary income.

That reality has kept questions about NFL cheerleader pay alive for years. In 2014, a New York Jets cheerleader filed a lawsuit alleging she was paid just $3.77 per hour. A year later, an Associated Press investigation reported that some NFL cheerleaders were earning less than fast-food workers.

The issue has received renewed attention in recent years, particularly following the arrival of Netflix’s “America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders” in 2024.

The push for better pay is gaining momentum

The documentary series offered viewers an inside look at the intense audition process, training, rehearsals and performances required of Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders. It also showed members balancing their NFL ambitions with school, professional careers and personal responsibilities.

The increased visibility helped fuel further conversations about compensation. In 2025, Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders secured a reported 400% pay increase, marking a major development in the long-running fight for better wages.

The change has also demonstrated how compensation can vary between NFL franchises. Reports following the increase indicated that veteran Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders could earn around $75 per hour under the new pay structure, depending on their assignments and schedules.

Still, a significant issue remains as cheerleaders are generally hired by individual NFL franchises rather than the league itself. That means teams have considerable control over their compensation and working arrangements, making league-wide changes more complicated.

Muscarello’s viral “double life” has become a reminder that the women performing under the stadium lights often have demanding careers away from football, too. As the 2026 NFL season gets underway, fans are increasingly asking whether those contributions are being valued fairly.

articles.title: NFL admits the referees favored Broncos in win over the Rams
articles.standfirst: The league acknowledged the penalty that extended Denver’s winning drive shouldn't have been called
articles.summary: The league acknowledged the penalty that extended Denver’s winning drive shouldn't have been called
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Rams already knew the final minutes of their loss to Denver Broncos had turned on one controversial flag. What they learned afterward was that the league agreed with them.

Coach Sean McVay said the NFL told the Rams that Josh Wallace shouldn't have been called for defensive pass interference on a late fourth-quarter play that erased his interception and kept the Broncos’ game-winning drive alive.

“They agreed with me,” McVay said Wednesday. The sequence came with Los Angeles leading 26-23 and Denver facing third-and-6 in the red zone.

Bo Nix threw toward Pat Bryant near the right sideline, and Wallace appeared to come down with the interception. Then came the flag.

Call completely changed the final minute

The penalty wiped out Wallace ’s interception and gave Denver a fresh set of downs.

Six plays later, Nix scored to put the Broncos ahead 30-26 with 47 seconds remaining. The Rams got the ball back but could not produce a final answer.

The frustration around the call only grew when Bryant later acknowledged that he made sure the contact looked obvious enough to draw a flag.

“It was a little pass interference, I did sell it just enough to get the flag,” Bryant told CBS Colorado. “He definitely gave me a little nudge that I felt, I felt like I couldn’t get the ball so it was either the ball or the call and we ended up with the call.”

Asked whether there is an art to selling contact in football, Bryant didn't shy away from the idea.

“Oh, yeah, of course,” he said. “It’s something that a lot of people do in this league.”

Wallace , unsurprisingly, saw the play differently: “It was very frustrating,” he said after the game.

McVay refuses to let mistake define loss

The NFL’s admission gives the Rams some vindication, but McVay has made a point of not turning the officiating error into an excuse: “We’re not going to play the victim,” he said earlier in the week.

Los Angeles had several chances to take control before the controversial finish. The Rams blew a 16-0 halftime lead, committed other costly penalties and allowed Denver to seize momentum after Matthew Stafford threw a pick-six.

McVay said the real value of the league’s feedback is in how it helps coaches instruct players going forward.

“The goal is just to get good, consistent feedback,” he said. “The only thing that matters to me is how to educate my players.”

He also made clear that Wallace ’s technique was not something he intended to change based on the play. The damage, however, is already done.

Denver improved to 2-1, while the Rams dropped to 1-2 after a game in which one of the biggest moments was ultimately officiated incorrectly.

The league’s admission cannot rewrite the result. It does confirm that Los Angeles had every reason to question the call that helped decide it.

articles.title: Broncos reporter leaves Sean Payton embarrassed after revealing what he thought was a cigarette
articles.standfirst: There was a more personal reason behind the head coach's reaction
articles.summary: There was a more personal reason behind the head coach's reaction
articles.body:
Sean Payton has experienced just about everything an NFL head coach can encounter during a postgame press conference. But after the Denver Broncos defeated the Carolina Panthers on Sunday, the veteran coach found himself in an unexpectedly awkward situation involving what he thought was a cigarette.

Moments after Denver secured a 26-21 victory over Carolina, Payton interrupted his postgame media session to address a reporter whom he believed was smoking inside the room. There was just one problem: The reporter wasn’t holding a cigarette. It was a pencil.

The 62-year-old coach quickly realized his mistake, apologized and laughed at the misunderstanding, turning what could have been an uncomfortable exchange into one of the more unusual moments of his postgame press conferences. “Could we not smoke in here? Please?” Payton initially asked.

However, after taking a closer look, he immediately corrected himself. “Oh, you’re not smoking. You got a pencil. I’m sorry. I thought you were smoking. I owe you,” Sean said, laughing. He then explained what had prompted the unusual interruption. “I had a flashback, thinking, who’s smoking a cigarette? All right. I’m sorry,” he added.

A sensitive topic for Sean Payton

While the exchange provided an amusing moment for those in attendance, there was a more personal reason behind Payton’s reaction. The Broncos coach lost his mother, Jean Jeanne Payton, to lung cancer, making the sight of someone potentially smoking a cigarette particularly sensitive for him.

The incident also offered another glimpse into Sean’s willingness to acknowledge his mistakes rather than turn a minor misunderstanding into a bigger confrontation. That approach was evident in October, when a reporter told him that an earlier interaction had made him come across as rude. Payton didn’t attempt to defend his behavior.

“I did not mean it. Yes, I did not mean that. No, I was just freaking tired and cranky,” he admitted. This time, the apology came much faster, thanks to a pencil that briefly looked like something else.

Broncos head into bye week with momentum

The unusual press conference moment came after another dramatic Denver victory, one that continued to reinforce the Broncos’ growing reputation as one of the NFL’s most resilient teams . Denver overcame a fourth-quarter deficit to defeat Carolina 26-21, improving to 7-2 and extending its winning streak to five games.

More impressively, the victory extended an extraordinary run in close games. The Broncos have now won 16 consecutive games decided by one score, an NFL record that highlights their ability to find ways to win even when the outcome remains uncertain until the final minutes.

Denver’s success has become particularly noticeable after an uneven start to the 2026 campaign. Last season, the Broncos finished 14-3, captured the AFC West and earned the conference’s No. 1 playoff seed. Expectations were consequently high, but the team needed time to establish its rhythm this year.

One significant adjustment came when Payton assumed play-calling responsibilities from Davis Webb. Since that change, Denver has won five consecutive games, giving the Broncos considerable momentum heading into their bye week.

Payton now intends to use the break to give his healthy players an opportunity to recover before beginning preparations for their next opponent, the Las Vegas Raiders.

Payton has more than one reason to smile

For Payton, the Carolina victory represented another important step toward establishing Denver as a legitimate contender in the AFC. The Broncos are riding a five-game winning streak, have improved to 7-2 and continue to demonstrate an ability to win tight contests. Their next challenge will be against the Raiders, with Payton hoping that a refreshed roster and continued control of the offense can keep the momentum going.

But Sunday also delivered a reminder that even experienced NFL coaches can find themselves caught in unexpected situations. Payton went into the press conference ready to discuss another hard-fought victory. Instead, he briefly became convinced that someone was smoking a cigarette in the room.

Fortunately, the suspected cigarette turned out to be nothing more than a pencil, and the coach was more than willing to admit he had gotten it wrong.

articles.title: Sean Payton shuts down ‘loophole’ talk, but Broncos still have a defensive problem without Henley
articles.standfirst: Denver must move forward without the linebacker they hoped would strengthen their defense
articles.summary: Denver must move forward without the linebacker they hoped would strengthen their defense
articles.body:
Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton isn’t interested in fueling the controversy surrounding the team’s failed attempt to acquire Los Angeles Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley . But he made one thing clear: Denver doesn’t believe it exploited a loophole in the NFL’s trade rules.

Speaking during his regular Monday morning news conference, Payton pushed back against Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh’s criticism of the trade process , which allowed Denver to seek revised compensation after Henley failed his physical. “I saw it all. There’s no loophole,” Payton said. “It just is part of the trade process every step of the way.”

“I saw it all. There’s no loophole,” Payton said. “It just is part of the trade process every step of the way.” The deal initially appeared to be a significant move for Denver, which was prepared to send a fourth- and fifth-round pick to Los Angeles in exchange for the linebacker. However, the agreement fell apart after Henley reportedly failed his physical in Denver because of concerns surrounding his knee.

The Broncos then sought to amend the compensation package, reportedly offering a fourth-round pick and an additional selection rather than the original fourth- and fifth-round combination. That change created friction between the AFC West rivals, and the trade was ultimately canceled.

Harbaugh described the situation as a “loophole” in the NFL rulebook, arguing that Denver had an opportunity to revisit the terms after the trade deadline had passed, leaving the Chargers with limited alternatives.

Payton, however, offered little support for that interpretation

Asked what had changed between the initial agreement and the deal falling apart, the Broncos coach insisted that the process had been clear from the beginning. “Nothing changed. It was already stated,” Payton said Monday.

“Everything was pretty clearly spelled out. I’m not going to get into the specifics. He’s a prospect we thought, and still do [think], very highly of. It just didn’t work out and it’s not uncommon with trades. That’s kind of where it went, and I’ll leave it at that.”

Both organizations reportedly contacted the NFL office after Henley failed his physical. Denver wanted clarification about its rights to request different compensation, while Los Angeles sought confirmation that the Broncos could make that request. The discussions did not produce an agreement, and the transaction was abandoned.

The controversy intensified when Henley returned to Los Angeles and practiced in full on Thursday and Friday without apparent restrictions. His quick return raised questions among fans about the severity of the knee concerns that had reportedly prompted Denver to reconsider the deal.

Denver’s interest in Henley was genuine

Still, the difference between the Chargers’ assessment and the Broncos’ medical evaluation remains unclear. Neither team’s public comments have provided a complete explanation of what happened during the physical, leaving plenty of room for speculation.

Payton’s comments did, however, reinforce that Denver’s interest in Henley was genuine. The Broncos viewed the linebacker as more than a temporary addition, which helps explain why they were willing to part with multiple draft selections in the original agreement.

That interest could become relevant again if Henley and the Chargers cannot reach a new contract before the start of the next league year in March. Denver could then explore pursuing him in free agency, although any potential move would depend on his market and the team’s plans.

For now, the Broncos must move forward without the linebacker they hoped would strengthen their defense.

Denver still has a linebacker problem to solve

The failed transaction is behind Denver, but the defensive need that motivated it has not disappeared. Entering Week 10, the Broncos had allowed the most receiving yards to running backs in the NFL and the second-most receiving yards to tight ends. Those numbers highlighted a vulnerability in coverage that Denver had hoped Henley could help address.

Now defensive coordinator Vance Joseph must find another solution with the players already on the roster. The timing is important, too. Denver returns from its bye week to face the Las Vegas Raiders , a division rival whose offense has shown a willingness to involve tight ends and running backs in the passing game.

Whether Kirk Cousins or Fernando Mendoza is leading the Raiders’ offense, Denver will need to be prepared for those matchups. The Broncos may have avoided a controversial trade, but they still have a problem to fix.

Payton can dismiss the idea of a loophole, and the Broncos can move on from the negotiations. The more pressing question is whether Denver can address its coverage issues without the player it worked so hard to acquire.

articles.title: Tom Jackson cause of death: Broncos legend dies at 75
articles.standfirst: The three-time Pro Bowl linebacker and longtime ESPN studio analyst passed away unexpectedly on Friday
articles.summary: The three-time Pro Bowl linebacker and longtime ESPN studio analyst passed away unexpectedly on Friday
articles.body:
Football fans and colleagues across the sports media landscape are in mourning following the death of former Denver Broncos star and Hall of Fame broadcaster Tom Jackson , who passed away on Friday at the age of 75.

ESPN senior NFL insider Adam Schefter broke the news on Sunday morning after Jackson’s family notified the network of his passing.

While reports described his death as sudden, neither his relatives, ESPN, nor the Broncos have publicly disclosed an official cause of death. He is survived by his wife, Jennifer , and his two daughters, Taylor and Morgan.

Long before millions of viewers welcomed him into their living rooms every autumn weekend, Jackson established himself as the fiery heart of one of the NFL’s most iconic defensive units.

Drafted by Denver in the fourth round out of the University of Louisville in 1973, the undersized yet relentless linebacker earned a full-time starting role by his second season and spent all 14 years of his playing career in a Broncos uniform before retiring after the 1986 campaign.

Across 191 regular-season contests and 10 playoff appearances, he amassed 1,531 tackles, 44 sacks, and 20 interceptions, returning three for touchdowns, while anchoring the famed “Orange Crush” defense that carried Denver to its inaugural Super Bowl appearance following the 1977 season.

A three-time Pro Bowler who was inducted into the Denver Broncos Ring of Fame in 1992, Jackson later revealed that the camaraderie forged in that locker room remained his proudest achievement.

From the “Orange Crush” defense to a Hall of Fame partnership at ESPN

Immediately after hanging up his cleats, Jackson pivoted to television in 1987 and embarked on a remarkable 29-year run with ESPN that forever changed how fans consumed NFL highlights and analysis.

Teaming up with anchor Chris Berman on “Sunday NFL Countdown” and “NFL Primetime,” Jackson blended sharp tactical breakdowns with infectious warmth and booming laughter.

Their chemistry proved so foundational to the network’s identity that ESPN eventually named its Bristol, Connecticut headquarters facility the Chris Berman-Tom Jackson Studio, still the only named studio on the company’s campus.

During Sunday morning’s broadcast of “Sunday NFL Countdown,” an emotional Berman shared the news of his longtime partner’s passing with viewers and reflected on their three decades together behind the desk.

“All of us are stunned,” Berman said in a statement. “I’m stunned, we’re stunned and you’re stunned. We’ve lost one of the best human beings ever to walk the planet, Tom Jackson. I was fortunate to work side by side with Tom for 30 years, primarily on NFL Primetime and Sunday NFL Countdown. It was a labor of love for our whole team, both in front of the camera and behind it. We always hoped our viewers enjoyed the shows as much as we did bringing it to them every week.”

Over the course of his broadcasting career, Jackson captured seven Sports Emmy Awards and earned the Pro Football Hall of Fame’s prestigious Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award in 2015, five years after Berman received the same distinction.

Although Jackson stepped away from full-time television duties following his coverage of the 2016 Pro Football Hall of Fame enshrinement ceremony, he briefly returned alongside Berman in 2019 for a digital-only edition of “NFL Primetime.”

In Denver, franchise officials announced through the team’s chief communications officer that the organization will honor Jackson with a pregame moment of silence and a tribute video prior to Sunday evening’s game against the Las Vegas Raiders .

In an official statement released Sunday, the team remembered both his grit on the turf and his enduring bond with the city.

“The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson , a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history,” the organization wrote in a statement Sunday.

“An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos’ first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos country.

“TJ’s dynamic personality, quick wit and football knowledge made him a natural for television and paved the way for a Hall of Fame broadcasting career.

For generations of fans, Tom was an iconic fixture on ESPN’s Sunday NFL Countdown and NFL Primetime, sharing his thoughtful insight with an unmistakable sense of humor that defined an era of sports broadcasting.

“Above all, TJ loved the Broncos and was a cherished member of our family for more than 50 years. We extend our deepest sympathies to Tom’s wife, Jennifer, his daughters, Taylor and Morgan, and all of his family, friends and teammates.”
paragraphs: Football fans and colleagues across the sports media landscape are in mourning following the death of former Denver Broncos star and Hall of Fame broadcaster Tom Jackson , who passed away on Friday at the age of 75.
ESPN senior NFL insider Adam Schefter broke the news on Sunday morning after Jackson’s family notified the network of his passing.

While reports described his death as sudden, neither his relatives, ESPN, nor the Broncos have publicly disclosed an official cause of death. He is survived by his wife, Jennifer , and his two daughters, Taylor and Morgan.
Long before millions of viewers welcomed him into their living rooms every autumn weekend, Jackson established himself as the fiery heart of one of the NFL’s most iconic defensive units.

Drafted by Denver in the fourth round out of the University of Louisville in 1973, the undersized yet relentless linebacker earned a full-time starting role by his second season and spent all 14 years of his playing career in a Broncos uniform before retiring after the 1986 campaign.

Across 191 regular-season contests and 10 playoff appearances, he amassed 1,531 tackles, 44 sacks, and 20 interceptions, returning three for touchdowns, while anchoring the famed “Orange Crush” defense that carried Denver to its inaugural Super Bowl appearance following the 1977 season.
A three-time Pro Bowler who was inducted into the Denver Broncos Ring of Fame in 1992, Jackson later revealed that the camaraderie forged in that locker room remained his proudest achievement.
From the “Orange Crush” defense to a Hall of Fame partnership at ESPN
Immediately after hanging up his cleats, Jackson pivoted to television in 1987 and embarked on a remarkable 29-year run with ESPN that forever changed how fans consumed NFL highlights and analysis.
Teaming up with anchor Chris Berman on “Sunday NFL Countdown” and “NFL Primetime,” Jackson blended sharp tactical breakdowns with infectious warmth and booming laughter.

Their chemistry proved so foundational to the network’s identity that ESPN eventually named its Bristol, Connecticut headquarters facility the Chris Berman-Tom Jackson Studio, still the only named studio on the company’s campus.

During Sunday morning’s broadcast of “Sunday NFL Countdown,” an emotional Berman shared the news of his longtime partner’s passing with viewers and reflected on their three decades together behind the desk.

“All of us are stunned,” Berman said in a statement. “I’m stunned, we’re stunned and you’re stunned. We’ve lost one of the best human beings ever to walk the planet, Tom Jackson. I was fortunate to work side by side with Tom for 30 years, primarily on NFL Primetime and Sunday NFL Countdown. It was a labor of love for our whole team, both in front of the camera and behind it. We always hoped our viewers enjoyed the shows as much as we did bringing it to them every week.”

Over the course of his broadcasting career, Jackson captured seven Sports Emmy Awards and earned the Pro Football Hall of Fame’s prestigious Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award in 2015, five years after Berman received the same distinction.

Although Jackson stepped away from full-time television duties following his coverage of the 2016 Pro Football Hall of Fame enshrinement ceremony, he briefly returned alongside Berman in 2019 for a digital-only edition of “NFL Primetime.”

In Denver, franchise officials announced through the team’s chief communications officer that the organization will honor Jackson with a pregame moment of silence and a tribute video prior to Sunday evening’s game against the Las Vegas Raiders .
In an official statement released Sunday, the team remembered both his grit on the turf and his enduring bond with the city.

“The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson , a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history,” the organization wrote in a statement Sunday.

“An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos’ first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos country.
“TJ’s dynamic personality, quick wit and football knowledge made him a natural for television and paved the way for a Hall of Fame broadcasting career.

For generations of fans, Tom was an iconic fixture on ESPN’s Sunday NFL Countdown and NFL Primetime, sharing his thoughtful insight with an unmistakable sense of humor that defined an era of sports broadcasting.

“Above all, TJ loved the Broncos and was a cherished member of our family for more than 50 years. We extend our deepest sympathies to Tom’s wife, Jennifer, his daughters, Taylor and Morgan, and all of his family, friends and teammates.”

articles.title: Heartbreaking details emerge about Tom Jackson's final days: Sudden silence, unanswered messages, and back surgery
articles.standfirst: The ESPN legend stopped responding shortly before his unexpected death at 75
articles.summary: The ESPN legend stopped responding shortly before his unexpected death at 75
articles.body:
For years, Bob Swenson could count on hearing from Tom Jackson almost every week, sometimes speaking with his former Denver Broncos teammate daily. That regular contact makes the silence in the days before Jackson 's unexpected death particularly difficult to understand.

Jackson , the three-time Pro Bowl linebacker who became one of ESPN's most recognizable NFL analysts, died Friday, November 20, at the age of 75, leaving former colleagues and friends struggling to comprehend the loss.

His family confirmed his passing, but an official cause of death has not been disclosed. Details subsequently shared by Swenson have offered a glimpse into Jackson 's final days, including conversations about ongoing physical problems and a possible operation.

"Unexpected. I talked to him every week, sometimes every day," Swenson told journalist Chris Tomasson while recalling their friendship.

The former Broncos linebacker explained that Jackson had been dealing with problems involving his back and leg, although there has been no confirmation that either condition contributed to his death.

Unanswered messages caused concern

Swenson , who played alongside Jackson in Denver from 1975 until 1983, said they had discussed the possibility of back surgery before communication between them unexpectedly stopped.

"I talked to him and he was going back and forth about getting a back operation and then he said he was going to do it," Swenson recalled.

"I would send him stuff and he came back and said, 'That's funny.' I won't say what the joke was."

However, the subsequent silence became increasingly troubling as Swenson attempted to check on his friend's condition.

"I was just waiting to hear back [about the surgery]. I texted him, 'Are you OK?' I think I texted him on Thursday and Friday and no response. … I was just stunned [at learning of his death]," he said.

NFL community mourn beloved ESPN broadcaster

Jackson spent his entire 14-season NFL career with Denver, becoming an important member of the franchise's celebrated Orange Crush defense before retiring in 1986.

His broadcasting career proved equally influential, particularly through his partnership with Chris Berman on ESPN's NFL Primetime and Sunday NFL Countdown.

The pair worked together for approximately three decades, developing a broadcasting relationship remembered for its chemistry, humor and understanding of professional football.

"All of us are stunned," Berman said in a statement following Jackson's death. "I'm stunned, we're stunned and you're stunned. We've lost one of the best human beings ever to walk the planet, Tom Jackson."

Tributes also came from broadcasters across the NFL, with CBS, Fox and NBC recognizing Jackson during Sunday's pregame programming.

The Broncos honored their former linebacker with a moment of silence and video tribute, while coach Sean Payton announced that a game ball would be presented to Jackson 's family.

For those who knew him personally, however, the loss extended far beyond his accomplishments in football and television.
